title: String Quartet No. 1 in E minor, “From My Life”
hook: A deaf composer tells his life story in four movements, right up to the high, whistling note that announced his deafness.

painting.title: Moonscape
painting.pairingNote: A Bohemian pond lies perfectly still under the moon, without a ripple; Smetana wrote this quartet in the silence of deafness, looking back over his life.

facts: In 1874 Smetana, then the leading Czech composer and chief conductor of Prague’s Provisional Theatre, began to hear a ringing in his ears. Within months he was completely deaf. In 1876 he moved out of Prague to Jabkenice, a village in the forests of central Bohemia, to live with his eldest daughter’s family.

There, between the autumn and 29 December 1876, he wrote this quartet. He called it a private piece, “four instruments conversing among themselves” about the things that tormented him. The noise in his ears let him work for only about an hour at a time.

In a letter to his friend Josef Srb-Debrnov he explained each movement: youth and a warning of misfortune, the dances of his young days, his first love, and the joy of creating Czech music, cut short by deafness.
Players at first found it too difficult. It was tried out privately in Prague with Antonín Dvořák playing the viola, and first performed in public on 29 March 1879, at the Konvikt hall in Prague.
bigPicture.inOneLine: the call of fate (I), a polka from his dancing youth (II), a love song (III), the joy of Czech music, broken by a piercing high note (IV).

movements.heading: Allegro vivo appassionato
movements.summary: It opens with a cry: a sharp chord, a restless trembling in the violins, and a passionate solo for the viola, which Smetana called “the call of fate into the struggle of life”. The movement is about his young self, he wrote: a love of art, romantic longings “for something I could not express”, and a warning of the misfortune to come.

mainIdeas.name: The viola’s theme
mainIdeas.description: a bold, aching melody that starts with a leap, played by the viola alone over agitated accompaniment.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: a warmer, more hopeful tune in G major, Smetana’s “inclination towards romanticism in music and in love”.

stops.hear: A sharp chord; the violins quiver on two notes; the viola sings a passionate, leaping melody
stops.happening: Theme 1: “the call of fate”, on the viola

stops.hear: A hard chord from all four breaks off the viola’s song; the music grows more urgent
The tension eases: a warmer, more hopeful melody
The themes are thrown about, louder and more troubled
The warm second theme returns, but the viola’s opening theme does not
The opening ideas come back, more subdued

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The music grows quieter and ends softly

notice: A quartet usually begins with the first violin. Here the viola, the quartet’s inner voice, gets the opening tune. At the first private play-through, the viola player was Dvořák.

movements.heading: Allegro moderato à la Polka
movements.summary: A [[polka|polka]], the Czech dance Smetana grew up with. He wrote that it took him back to “the joyful days of youth”, when he wrote dance music and was known as a passionate dancer, among country people and in elegant salons. There are three kinds of dance here: a sturdy country polka, a trumpet-like call on the viola, and a gentler salon dance in the middle.

mainIdeas.name: The polka
mainIdeas.description: a strong, bouncy dance tune, first with all four playing together.

mainIdeas.name: The call
mainIdeas.description: a contrasting figure on the viola, marked “quasi tromba”, like a trumpet.

mainIdeas.name: The middle section
mainIdeas.description: the viola and cello keep a polka rhythm while the violins play smooth chords above.

stops.hear: All four play a bold, bouncing dance tune together
The viola plays a brassy figure, like a trumpet at a village dance
Slower and smoother: a gentle swing in the low strings, sweet chords in the violins
stops.happening: The middle section, a more elegant dance

stops.hear: The country polka returns, shorter
A brief memory of the gentle middle dance

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: The dance whirls to a forceful end

notice: Listen to the viola’s “trumpet” calls. String instruments rarely try to imitate brass so openly.

movements.heading: Largo sostenuto
movements.summary: A love song for Kateřina Kolářová, Smetana’s first wife, who died in 1859. He wrote that it recalls “the happiness of my first love for the girl who later became my faithful wife”. It opens with a solo for the cello, then the first violin sings the main melody. The music grows into a passionate struggle before it settles again into a quiet, reflective end.

mainIdeas.name: The cello’s opening
mainIdeas.description: a long, searching phrase, alone at first.

mainIdeas.name: The love theme
mainIdeas.description: a tender, singing melody in A-flat major for the first violin.

mainIdeas.name: The second melody
mainIdeas.description: different in shape but just as ardent.

stops.hear: The cello alone, a warm, searching phrase
The first violin sings a tender, flowing melody
stops.happening: The love theme, in A-flat major

stops.hear: A second melody, just as warm, passed between the instruments
The music swells, more and more passionate and troubled
stops.happening: “The struggle with an unkind fate”, in Smetana’s words

stops.hear: The calm returns, and the love theme comes back

stops.label: Last 90 seconds
stops.hear: Slower and softer; the music fades into stillness

notice: Smetana wrote that the players of his day thought this movement impossible to perform. Listen to how high and exposed the lines are, especially for the first violin.

movements.heading: Vivace
movements.summary: The finale celebrates what Smetana called “the discovery that I could treat national elements in music”, with a lively, folk-like dance. Then, near the end, everything stops. Over a shivering [[tremolo|tremolo]], the first violin plays a long, piercing high E: the whistling in his ears that in 1874 announced his deafness. Fragments of the first movement drift back, and the quartet ends in resignation.

mainIdeas.name: The dance
mainIdeas.description: a bright, quick folk-like tune in E major, full of energy.

mainIdeas.name: The high E
mainIdeas.description: a long, thin, whistling note in [[harmonics|harmonics]] on the first violin.

mainIdeas.name: The memories
mainIdeas.description: a quiet return of ideas from the first movement.

stops.hear: A quick, bright, dancing tune
stops.happening: The finale’s main theme: joy in Czech music

stops.hear: A second, lilting tune
The dance tunes are developed, more and more exuberant
The opening dance returns
A sudden chord and silence; then a trembling in the middle strings and a long, piercing high note on the first violin
stops.happening: The high E: the sound of his tinnitus

stops.hear: Quiet memories of the first movement’s themes

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: Soft, resigned chords, with a glimmer of warmth
stops.happening: “A little ray of hope”, Smetana wrote

notice: The high E is not an effect for its own sake. Smetana wrote that he allowed himself this “little joke” because the sound had been so fateful for him. (The noise he actually heard was a high chord, not a single note.)

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: The Pavel Haas Quartet, from Prague, recorded both Smetana quartets in 2014; the album won the 2015 Gramophone Award for chamber music.

threads.title: Music as autobiography
threads.body: Smetana gave each movement a chapter of his life. A programme like this was then very unusual in a string quartet; it later inspired Janáček’s two programmatic quartets.

threads.title: The warning
threads.body: The misfortune announced in the first movement arrives in the last, as the high E. Smetana said the long note in the finale grew out of the warning at the beginning.

threads.title: Czech voice
threads.body: The polka, the folk-like finale and the joy in “national elements” make this one of the first great Czech chamber works.
